title: Fatha: the "a" sound, full letter × fatha grid
objectives: Student can explain that a fatha (a small diagonal stroke above a letter) makes that letter produce a short "a" sound immediately after its consonant sound.
Student can read any of the 28 letters + fatha on sight, in randomized order (the full letter × fatha grid, 28 cells).

Student notices (with teacher prompting) that the "a" sound changes quality — darker/backed toward "o" — after a heavy letter (ص ض ط ظ ق غ خ), as a first sensory exposure to tafkheem-affecting-the-vowel, ahead of the formal Phase 3 rule.

slides.heading: Lesson 1.10 — Fatha: the "a" sound, full letter × fatha grid
Every letter, ten-fold
body: Ibn Mas'ud reported the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as saying: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of Allah, he will have a reward, and that reward will be multiplied by ten. I do not say that Alif-Lam-Mim is one letter, but Alif is a letter, Lam is a letter, and Mim is a letter." (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2910, Hasan)
Starting today, every one of the 28 letters carries its own vowel sound — each one still carries that same ten-fold reward, letter by letter.

slides.heading: Recap — full 28-letter shuffle + a couple of Unit 1.2 clusters

audio.cue: ا: an open, unobstructed sound from deep in the chest cavity — no closure anywhere, just a clear open vowel
lips fully together
tongue-tip on gum ridge
tongue between teeth
ح: a strong, breathy, unvoiced friction from the middle of the throat — like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat, no English equivalent
خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened
د: tongue-tip taps the upper gum ridge firmly — a plain, crisp 'd'
ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

audio.title: Arabic101 Makharij Lesson 10 — ر (ra), the ULTIMATE guide

audio.cue: ز: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, a plain buzzing 'z' — voiced twin of س
س: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, a thin hiss — a plain 's'
ش: middle of tongue against the roof of the mouth, a soft 'sh'
ع: a mid-throat muscular squeeze, voiced — no equivalent sound in English or Turkic languages
غ: upper throat, same zone as خ but voiced — a uvular fricative, like a French uvular 'r'
ف: inner lower lip against the edge of the upper front teeth — a plain 'f'
ك: back of tongue against the soft palate, shallower in the mouth than ق — a plain 'k'
م: the two lips, with nasal resonance — 'm'
ه: a light, breathy throat release — a soft 'h', much gentler than ح
و: rounded lips — a consonant 'w'
ي: middle of tongue toward the roof of the mouth — a consonant 'y'
Read بتث aloud, letter by letter: ba + ta + tha — then blend them smoothly.
Read دذر aloud, letter by letter: dal + dhal + ra — then blend them smoothly.

slides.heading: Harakat — marks that add a vowel sound
body: Harakat are small marks placed above or below a letter that tell you which short vowel sound follows the consonant.
Today's mark is fatha ( ﹷ ), a short "a".

Note: alif's own vowel-grid cell is conventionally written as أَ (alif carrying hamza + fatha), since bare alif does not itself carry a short-vowel mark in real orthography — a teaching convention, not a new letter.

slides.heading: Worked example: بَ
body: بَ (ba + fatha) — sounded out slowly: "b" + short "a".

audio.cue: بَ + fatha: the two lips (shafatan), fully closed, vowel a

slides.heading: Worked example: تَ, ثَ
body: Same pattern, dotted family: تَ (ta + fatha), ثَ (tha + fatha).

audio.cue: تَ + fatha: tip of tongue against the upper front teeth / gum ridge, vowel a
ثَ + fatha: tip of tongue between the teeth (interdental), vowel a

slides.heading: A heavy letter: صَ
body: Same fatha mark, but notice the "a" now sounds fuller/darker ("saw"-like, not flat "sa") — this is your first taste of tafkheem (the heavier, fuller quality some letters give their vowels).
Say سَ then صَ back to back to feel the difference.

audio.cue: سَ + fatha: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, thin hiss, vowel a
صَ + fatha: same point as س, but back of tongue raised, mouth cavity fuller — heavy twin of س, vowel a

dailyChecklist: Write today's marked syllables (28-cell grid) 4 rows each in your notebook, saying each sound aloud as you write
Randomized-order self-quiz drill: read each cell aloud
Review previously learned letters via the cumulative shuffle
Listen once to the fatha section of the Muallimi Soniy compilation video — use its own chapter list to find that section

script: Open with the Tirmidhi 2910 hadith (reward ×10 per letter, Alif-Lam-Mim) — today every letter starts carrying its own vowel, so frame it as the reward multiplying letter by letter.
Introduce fatha as a short, crisp 'a' — model بَ/تَ/ثَ slowly, exaggerating that the vowel is SHORT, never lengthened into a madd.
Demonstrate the heavy-letter darkening explicitly on صَ — say سَ then صَ back to back so the 'a' vs fuller/darker 'a' contrast is unmistakable.

Since no vetted 'hear the whole grid' video is wired in yet (candidates are unverified/audition-required per verified-resources.md §4), demonstrate the full 28-cell grid live yourself, at natural pace, before the randomized re-drill.
Run the grid in its natural order first (two guided halves), then re-drill fully randomized — the randomized pass is the real recognition test, not the ordered one.
Close with the heavy-vs-light contrast pairs, listening specifically for whether the 'a' darkens correctly after ص ط ظ ق.
listenFor: Fatha lengthened into a full madd ("aa" instead of a short "a") — this is the single most common vowel-timing error and matters enormously later (madd rules are a major Phase 3 unit); catch it here at the source.

Heavy letters' fatha not darkening at all (student produces a flat "a" even after ص ض ط ظ ق غ خ) — the first testable instance of the tafkheem-bleeds-into-the-vowel pattern named in the sourced research (teaching-mistakes-assessment.md A.2).

Any regression on the underlying consonant sound now that a vowel is attached (a letter that was solid in isolation coming out wrong once voweled) — re-flag using the same high-risk-six watchlist from Unit 1.1.

Daily heavy-vs-light contrast pairs (4 pairs × 3 reps). Review previously learned letters via the cumulative shuffle.
